name: Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah (al-Zir Salim)
bio: Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah, called al-Zir Salim, was a chief of the tribe of Taghlib in northern Arabia in the later sixth century. He was the brother of Kulaib, the Taghlibite leader whose killing set off the War of Basus, the long feud between Taghlib and its kinsmen of Bakr. Muhalhil took up the vengeance and is remembered in Arab tradition as the avenger who fought that war for decades.

Tradition also names him as one of the first poets to lengthen the qasida, and a small body of verse is ascribed to him, chiefly laments for Kulaib and boasts of the fighting. The elegy here is Reynold A. Nicholson's English version, from his Translations of Eastern Poetry and Prose (1922); no Arabic original is given.

poems.title: Elegy for Kulaib
poems.author: Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah (al-Zir Salim)
poems.collection: Translations of Eastern Poetry and Prose (1922)
poems.text:
O night we are passing at Dhu Husum, shine forth into dawn
  when thou art ended, and return not!
If my night at al-Dhana'ib hath been long, yet was I used
  to weep for the shortness of the night.
Meseems the Kid, the Kid of the Wain, sinks prone on his
  forelegs in a rolling sky,
Whilst Sirius and his twin star creep towards Canopus, which
  gleams like the crown of an aged camel.
Were the graveyards dug up, so that Kulaib might be uncovered and know at al-Dhana'ib what a “visitor of
  women”
I proved myself on the day of al-Shu'batan, his eye would be
  gladdened—but how shall we meet them that are under
  the tombs?
And lo, at Waridat I have left Bujair in a flow of blood like
  the unguent mixed with saffron:
By slaying him I tore the tents of the Banu 'Ubad—and some
  deed of violence is most healing to stricken hearts—
Albeit he doth not pay fully for Kulaib, such a man as my
  brother was when the women rush forth from their
  bowers.
And Hammam son of Murra: him too we have left low, over
  him the huge male vulture,
Heaving up his breast in which the spear is fixed, while
  another great brute like a camel is tugging at him.
And were it not for the wind, those in Hajr would be made
  to hear the clang of helmets smitten by our swordblades.
My life for the Banu Shakika! the day they came like lions
  of the jungle that persevered in roaring,
As though their spears were the ropes of a deep well whose
  walls are wide apart,
On the morn when beside 'Unaiza we and the sons of our
  father were (grinding one another) as two mill-stones
  turned by hand,
And our horses standing over them all day, the horses
  (sweating) as though washed in a water-pool.
